faqs.question: What is the SENTERRA II Raman Microscope used for?
faqs.answer: The SENTERRA II is a confocal Raman microscope used for failure analysis, quality control, and scientific research, across pharmaceuticals, forensics, polymers, and environmental testing.

faqs.question: What is SureCal, and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: SureCal is a patented technology that continuously recalibrates the SENTERRA II in the background, holding sub-wavenumber precision without a manual recalibration step interrupting analysis.

faqs.question: Can the SENTERRA II identify unknown substances automatically?
faqs.answer: Yes, using A.I.D., an AI-driven tool that matches spectral data against reference databases in seconds, for pure substances or complex mixtures.

faqs.answer: Select a built-in laser with one click, place the sample under the microscope, and start the measurement. A.I.D. then runs the identification automatically against reference spectral databases, returning a match with diagnostics and hit-quality graphs in seconds.

faqs.question: Can it generate a chemical image without selecting a Raman peak first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Adaptive K-means Clustering sorts spectra into groups automatically and builds the chemical image on its own.

faqs.question: How do I generate a chemical image of a mixed or heterogeneous sample using the SENTERRA II?
faqs.answer: Run Adaptive K-means Clustering after the measurement, without selecting a specific Raman peak first. The software sorts the spectra into groups automatically and builds the chemical image on its own, showing at a glance whether the sample is homogeneous or structured.

faqs.question: Can the SENTERRA II be configured for live cell or tissue research?

faqs.question: Is the SENTERRA II suitable for a regulated pharmaceutical environment?

sections.title: How SureCal and Class 1 safety work together
body: Every Raman microscope drifts. Heat, component wear, and vibration all shift wavenumber accuracy over time, and most systems handle that with a scheduled recalibration routine that takes the instrument offline.

SureCal removes that step entirely, recalibrating continuously in the background so precision holds without a pause in analysis. That matters whether you're running a quick material identification or collecting a large dataset for PCA or other statistical work, where consistency across hundreds of measurements is the whole point.

Laser safety runs on the same always-on principle: the Class 1 housing and interlock protect the user in every operating mode, which is what makes SENTERRA II usable by students and first-time operators without a separate safety program.

faqs.question: What is random-walk imaging?
faqs.answer: Random-walk imaging is a search algorithm that finds and follows the Raman signal directly, rather than scanning a sample in a fixed pattern regardless of what's present.

faqs.question: How much faster is RAMANwalk than a conventional Raman microscope?

faqs.question: How do I check a sample for a specific contaminant quickly with the RAMANwalk?
faqs.answer: Run the random-walk search targeted at the contaminant's Raman signature rather than a full scan. On a comparable real sample, this reached a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes, versus roughly 50 minutes for a complete image.

faqs.question: Can RAMANwalk find signal in low-contrast samples?
faqs.answer: Yes. It locates regions of interest using chemical Raman information, even when the sample gives no useful visual contrast.

faqs.question: How many objective lenses does the RAMANwalk offer?
faqs.answer: Five: 5x, 10x, 20x, 50x, and 100x, covering broad overview imaging through fine sub-micron detail.

faqs.question: Does the RAMANwalk need manual calibration?
faqs.answer: No. It auto-calibrates against a standard lamp and sample, and auto-aligns its own optical path.

faqs.question: Is the RAMANwalk safe to use without laser safety training?

sections.eyebrow: Random Walk Imaging and Scan Speed
sections.title: How the algorithm finds an answer faster than a scan
body: A conventional Raman microscope treats every point in a sample as equally worth visiting. RAMANwalk doesn't.

The random-walk algorithm finds a distinctive Raman signal, searches the surrounding area for more of it, and moves rapidly elsewhere once the signal runs out. It's a fundamentally different search strategy, not just a faster version of the old one, and it's why RAMANwalk delivers a rough preview in under a minute and finer detail within a few minutes, well before a full scan would even be close to done.

On a real contamination question, that difference is the whole point: a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes, against a traditional raster scan that's only 10% complete in the same time, with nothing found yet.
